claims.claim: The 50% Capital Gains Tax discount has been completely abolished for all Australians.
claims.short_explanation: Abolished for assets acquired after 1 July 2027 only. Pre-existing assets use a hybrid system. SMSFs are fully exempt.
claims.detailed_explanation: The 50% CGT discount is not abolished for everyone. It applies only to assets acquired after 1 July 2027. Assets already held will use a hybrid calculation — the old 50% discount applies to gains accrued up to 30 June 2027, and CPI indexation applies after that date. Self-Managed Superannuation Funds (SMSFs) are entirely excluded and retain their one-third discount.

claims.claim: Negative gearing has been fully abolished in Australia.
claims.short_explanation: Negative gearing is NOT abolished. It is restricted for new buyers of established homes only. Three distinct pathways still allow deductions.
claims.detailed_explanation: Negative gearing has not been abolished. Existing property investors keep full deductions. New investors buying established homes post-budget lose the ability to offset rental losses against salary income (losses are quarantined). Investors in new builds retain full negative gearing. Three distinct rules apply depending on when and what you bought.

claims.claim: Self-Managed Super Funds (SMSFs) are completely exempt from the new CGT changes.
claims.short_explanation: Confirmed. SMSFs retain the existing one-third CGT discount and are not subject to the 30% minimum floor or indexation rules.
claims.detailed_explanation: The Treasury and ATO have confirmed SMSFs are carved out entirely from the new CGT framework. SMSFs continue to use the existing one-third discount on long-held assets. The 30% minimum tax floor does not apply to SMSF asset disposals. This is a deliberate policy exclusion to protect retirement savings structures.

claims.claim: Assets purchased before 1985 will lose their full CGT exemption.
claims.short_explanation: Confirmed. Pre-CGT assets (bought before 20 Sept 1985) will have their cost base reset via ATO market valuation on 1 July 2027, ending 42 years of CGT exemption.
claims.detailed_explanation: Assets acquired before 20 September 1985 — including share portfolios — have historically been exempt from Capital Gains Tax entirely. Under the 2026 budget, this legacy exemption ends. The ATO will establish a market valuation of these assets on 1 July 2027 to set a new cost base. Any gains after that date will be subject to the new CPI indexation and 30% floor rules.

claims.claim: These budget changes are already law and will definitely take effect on 1 July 2027.
claims.short_explanation: NOT yet law. Budget measures must pass both houses of parliament. Opposition has flagged a Senate challenge. Consult an accountant before making decisions.
claims.detailed_explanation: Budget announcements are not law. They require legislation to be passed by both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The Coalition opposition has indicated it will challenge key provisions in the Senate. Until legislation passes, these remain proposed changes only. Always verify the legal status of any tax change with a registered accountant before adjusting your financial strategy.

claims.claim: Inflation indexation always produces a better CGT outcome than the 50% discount for long-held assets.
claims.short_explanation: Inflation indexation does not guarantee a lower CGT liability. The 50% discount may be more favourable when inflation is high over the holding period, as indexation only adjusts the cost base upward, while the discount directly halves the total gain.
claims.detailed_explanation: While CPI indexation raises the cost base to reflect inflation, it doesn't reduce the taxable gain itself—only the discount method cuts the gain in half. With high inflation over extended periods, the indexed cost base may still leave a substantial taxable gain, making the 50% discount more advantageous in many scenarios.

claims.claim: From 1 July 2027, capital gains will be subject to a new minimum 30% tax rate on all gains.
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum rate applies to real capital gains after inflation indexation, not nominal gains. This means the effective tax rate on nominal gains may be substantially lower depending on inflation and the holding period.
claims.detailed_explanation: The headline '30% minimum tax on capital gains' can be misleading. The 30% floor rate applies to actual economic gains after accounting for inflation through indexation, not the nominal gain amount. For example, a $100,000 nominal gain might only be a $40,000 real gain after inflation adjustment, meaning tax would be 30% of $40,000 rather than $100,000. The effective tax rate on nominal gains can be significantly lower than 30% depending on inflation and how long the asset was held.

claims.claim: Division 296 imposes a 15% tax on all superannuation balances exceeding $3 million
claims.verdict_label: Disputed — tax applies to earnings above threshold only
claims.short_explanation: The 15% Division 296 tax does not apply to the entire balance above $3m. It only applies to the earnings (or proportion of income) that relate to the amount by which your Total Superannuation Balance exceeds the indexed Lump Sum Threshold.
claims.detailed_explanation: Division 296 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997, known as the 'Better Targeted Super Concessions' measure, introduces an additional 15% tax on 'income from superannuation' that relates to superannuation balances above the Lump Sum Threshold (LSBT). The $3 million threshold was set for the 2025-26 income year and is indexed annually in $100,000 increments. Critically, the tax is calculated on the 'proportion of income from superannuation that relates to the amount by which your Total Superannuation Balance exceeds the LSBT' — not on the balance itself or the excess amount in its entirety. This means a member with a $3.5 million balance does not pay 15% on the full $500,000 excess; rather, they pay 15% on the portion of their earnings attributable to that excess, with the calculation based on the income stream's proportion of the total balance that exceeds the threshold. This is a meaningful distinction that significantly affects the actual tax liability for affected members.

claims.detailed_explanation: The claim mischaracterises how Division 296 works. Rather than taxing the entire balance above $3m, or even the excess amount itself, Division 296 imposes 15% tax specifically on the earnings and returns (interest, dividends, capital gains) that relate to the portion of an individual's Total Superannuation Balance (TSB) that exceeds $3 million. For example, an individual with $4m in superannuation would only face the 15% tax on the investment returns generated by the $1m above the threshold, not on the $1m principal, the $4m total, or the earnings themselves.

claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum applies to inflation-indexed capital gains, not necessarily all nominal gains. Actual tax rates depend on the taxpayer's marginal rate.
claims.detailed_explanation: Media coverage often states that a flat 30% minimum applies to all capital gains, but the budget.gov.au tax reform page specifies 'a minimum 30% tax on gains' in the context of inflation indexation replacing the 50% general discount. The actual tax rate depends on the taxpayer's marginal rate, with indexation determining the taxable gain amount. For example, a taxpayer on the 47% marginal rate would pay 47% on indexed gains, not a flat 30%. The 30% minimum effectively applies when the indexed gain would otherwise be taxed at a lower rate. This oversimplification may mislead people about the actual impact on their personal tax situation.

claims.claim: Capital gains will face a minimum 30% tax rate on ALL gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum tax rate may only apply to gains above inflation, not to all capital gains.
claims.detailed_explanation: The official budget documentation describes a discount based on inflation, suggesting that the taxable portion would be calculated as (nominal gain - inflation adjustment), with the 30% floor applying only to that inflation-adjusted portion. This means gains that merely track inflation could face different treatment compared to gains significantly above inflation. The claim oversimplifies by suggesting all gains face a flat 30% minimum, when the mechanism appears more nuanced.

claims.claim: Negative gearing is restricted from Budget Night (12 May 2026)
claims.short_explanation: The 7:30pm Budget Night cutoff applies to new property purchases, but existing negatively-geared properties retain their status until 1 July 2027.
claims.detailed_explanation: While the government announced changes at 7:30pm on Budget Night (12 May 2026), this timing marks the cutoff for new property purchases to be affected by the restrictions. Existing negatively-geared properties maintain their current status and benefits until the changes take full effect on 1 July 2027. This creates an important distinction between the announcement/calculation cutoff date (7:30pm Budget Night) and the full implementation date (1 July 2027). Media reporting may conflate these dates, suggesting restrictions apply immediately when they actually target future purchases.

claims.claim: A retired investor on a 16% marginal tax rate 'faces 8% tax on nominal gains' under the current CGT system, as opposed to 30% on indexed gains.
claims.short_explanation: The 8% figure is mathematically correct (16% × 50% CGT discount = 8% effective rate), and the 30% on indexed gains reflects the old indexation method. However, the comparison is misleading because it presents these as fixed outcomes rather than alternative calculation methods taxpayers can choose between based on which produces the lower tax liability.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim's numbers are arithmetically accurate: under the current CGT system, individual investors on a 16% marginal tax rate who qualify for the 50% CGT discount face an effective rate of 8% on nominal capital gains. The 30% figure represents the tax on fully indexed gains at the old system (indexed cost base multiplied by 30% marginal rate). However, the claim creates a misleading comparison by treating these as the only two applicable rates. In reality, for assets acquired after 21 September 1999, taxpayers can choose between calculating CGT using the 50% discount method or the indexation method—whichever results in a lower tax liability. The actual outcome depends on the holding period and inflation during ownership. For short holding periods, the 50% discount typically produces lower CGT. For long-held assets with high inflation, indexation may produce a lower or comparable result. The ASX analysis correctly notes the dramatic 8% vs 30% comparison, but framing this as the 'choice' facing investors oversimplifies the decision-making process and may mislead readers about the relative burden of the current system.

claims.claim: Capital gains will face a new minimum 30% tax rate on ALL gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum rate applies to indexed (inflation-adjusted) gains above the cost base, not to total nominal gains.
claims.detailed_explanation: The 30% floor does not apply to total nominal gains as commonly reported. Under the new system, the cost base is first indexed to inflation, and only gains above this indexed threshold are subject to the minimum 30% rate. For example, an investor currently on a 16% marginal rate facing 8% tax on nominal gains would see those gains taxed at 30% on the indexed portion only. The indexation mechanism means that where significant inflation has occurred, the indexed cost base may be substantially higher, reducing the taxable gain. Investors in lower tax brackets or where indexation significantly reduces gains may face effective rates substantially different from 30%. The phrase 'on ALL gains' overstates the floor's actual application to indexed taxable gains only.

claims.claim: 15% tax on all super balances exceeding $3m
claims.short_explanation: The 15% tax under Division 296 applies to investment earnings attributable to the portion of superannuation balance exceeding the $3 million threshold, not the entire balance above $3 million.
claims.detailed_explanation: Division 296 (the Better Targeted Super Concessions measure) imposes a 15% tax on the proportion of earnings relating to an individual's Total Superannuation Balance (TSB) that exceeds the $3 million Low Balance Superannuation Account (LSBT) threshold. This is a crucial distinction from the commonly reported characterisation. For example, an individual with a $4 million balance would not be taxed on the entire $1 million above the threshold. Instead, the 15% tax applies only to the investment earnings generated on the $1 million excess portion. This means the actual tax liability depends on the earnings rate applied to the excess balance, not a flat 15% on the balance amount itself.

claims.claim: Inflation accounts for 56% of ASX 200 share gains over 10 years to March 2026
claims.short_explanation: Treasury and budget.gov.au data confirms the 56% figure, but it applies specifically to shares held for exactly 10 years and does not apply to property or other asset classes.
claims.detailed_explanation: The Treasury analysis cited in the 2026-27 Budget documents and by the ABC confirms that inflation accounted for 56% of ASX 200 asset price growth for shares held over the 10-year period to March 2026. This statistic is accurate as presented. However, important context is required: (1) The 56% figure refers to inflation's contribution to price growth, not total returns including dividends; (2) The figure applies specifically to shares held for exactly 10 years and may differ for shorter or longer holding periods; (3) This analysis is specific to ASX 200 shares and should not be applied to residential property or other asset classes, which have different inflation dynamics and tax treatments; (4) The figure should not be misrepresented as '56% of investment returns' more broadly.

claims.claim: 15% tax on all super balances over $3m
claims.short_explanation: Division 296 applies 15% tax only to the earnings attributable to the portion of a super balance exceeding $3m, not the entire balance above the threshold.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim conflates the tax base. According to the ATO, Division 296 tax is 15% on 'the proportion of earnings relating to your total superannuation balance (TSB) that exceeds the $3m threshold' — not on the balance itself. Media coverage often simplifies this to '15% on balances over $3m', which overstates the tax impact since only earnings (not principal) above the threshold are taxed. The $3m threshold is based on an individual's Total Superannuation Balance, and the 15% additional tax applies only to the share of income derived from assets that correspond to the amount above $3m.

claims.claim: A retired investor on a 16% marginal tax rate pays 8% effective tax on capital gains under current rules
claims.short_explanation: The 8% figure is mathematically correct (16% × 50% CGT discount = 8%), resulting from the standard 50% CGT discount available to all eligible taxpayers, not a special low rate.
claims.detailed_explanation: The ASX analysis correctly calculates that a retired investor on a 16% marginal tax rate faces an 8% effective tax rate on nominal capital gains. This results from applying the standard 50% CGT discount: 16% × 50% = 8%. However, media coverage often oversimplifies this as 'paying only 8% tax' without explaining the underlying discount mechanism. The 50% CGT discount applies to all eligible assets held for more than 12 months by eligible taxpayers—including individuals, trusts, and partnerships—not exclusively to retired investors. This comparison with the 30% rate for indexed gains highlights the preferential treatment of nominal versus indexed gains, but the 8% figure reflects the standard discount mechanism rather than a special low rate designed for retirees.

claims.claim: 15% tax on all super balances over $3m
claims.short_explanation: Division 296 taxes investment earnings, not the superannuation balance itself. The 15% tax applies only to the portion of earnings attributable to balances exceeding the $3m threshold.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim mischaracterises how Division 296 operates. Rather than imposing a flat 15% tax on the amount by which a superannuation balance exceeds $3 million, the tax applies specifically to 'taxable super earnings' (investment returns). The 15% levy is calculated on the proportion of those earnings that relate to the portion of an individual's Total Superannuation Balance (TSB) above the Low Balance Super Threshold (LSBT) of $3 million. For example, a $5 million balance would not attract a tax of $300,000 (15% × $2 million). Instead, the tax would be 15% of the investment earnings that can be attributed to the $2 million excess above the threshold. This distinction is significant because the actual liability depends on investment performance, not merely account size.

claims.claim: $2 billion infrastructure initiative will deliver 65,000 additional homes
claims.short_explanation: Government projections cite this target, but independent analysis questions whether it is achievable due to delivery capacity and methodology concerns.
claims.detailed_explanation: Multiple government sources cite the $2 billion infrastructure initiative as projected to deliver 65,000 additional homes. However, the Grattan Institute and independent analysts have disputed this figure, questioning whether the target is achievable. Concerns centre on delivery capacity constraints, methodology assumptions, and the failure to account for potential delays or infrastructure bottlenecks that could significantly reduce actual home delivery numbers. Independent modelling suggests actual delivery could fall well short of the 65,000 projection.

claims.claim: The government's $2 billion infrastructure initiative will deliver 65,000 additional homes
claims.short_explanation: While government sources cite 65,000 homes, Grattan Institute and independent analysis question whether the target is realistic or achievable.
claims.detailed_explanation: Multiple government sources cite the $2B infrastructure initiative as delivering 65,000 additional homes. However, Grattan Institute and independent modelling question whether this target is achievable. The $2B funding is tied to housing supply milestones, suggesting conditional rather than guaranteed delivery. Independent experts suggest the timeline and delivery mechanisms may not support such a specific figure.

claims.claim: The $2 billion infrastructure initiative will deliver 65,000 additional homes
claims.short_explanation: Independent analysis, including Grattan Institute modelling, questions whether this housing target is achievable, and the $2B figure may represent aspirational targets rather than guaranteed delivery.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim conflates infrastructure spending with guaranteed housing delivery. While the government has cited a 65,000 home figure in association with the $2 billion infrastructure initiative, independent modelling from the Grattan Institute raises significant questions about whether this target is realistic or achievable. The $2 billion in infrastructure funding may be tied to housing supply milestones rather than guaranteeing 65,000 new homes will be built. Housing delivery depends on multiple factors beyond infrastructure investment, including developer capacity, planning approvals, construction costs, and market conditions. The 65,000 figure should be understood as an aspirational target or upper estimate rather than a confirmed projection backed by independent verification.

claims.claim: Division 296 imposes a 15% tax on all superannuation balances exceeding $3 million
claims.short_explanation: Division 296 does not impose a flat 15% tax on the entire balance exceeding $3 million. Instead, it applies a 15% tax on the proportion of taxable superannuation earnings attributable to balances above the $3 million threshold.
claims.detailed_explanation: Division 296 of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Better Targeted Super Concessions) Act 2023 introduces an additional 15% tax on the taxable superannuation balance (TSB) that exceeds the $3 million Low Balance Super Account (LSBT) threshold. However, this is not a tax on the balance itself but rather on the earnings (income) generated by the portion of the balance that exceeds $3 million. For example, if someone has a $4 million super balance and earns $200,000 in a year, only the earnings attributable to the $1 million excess (proportionally) would be subject to the additional 15% tax, not the $1 million excess amount itself.

claims.claim: Inflation indexation always produces a better CGT outcome than the 50% discount for long-held assets
claims.short_explanation: The relative benefit of inflation indexation versus the 50% CGT discount depends on inflation rates, holding period, and marginal tax rate—it is not universally better.
claims.detailed_explanation: This absolute claim is mathematically false in certain scenarios. The actual outcome depends on three key factors: (1) the inflation rate during the holding period, (2) the taxpayer's marginal tax rate, and (3) how long the asset is held. For high-income earners with short holding periods and low inflation, the 50% discount may still be more favorable. While Treasury analysis citing that 'inflation accounts for 56% of ASX 200 gains over the decade' supports the potential benefit of indexation, this data does not prove that indexation 'always' outperforms the discount across all circumstances. Taxpayers should model both scenarios based on their specific situation rather than assuming one method is universally superior.

claims.claim: Division 296 imposes a 15% tax on all superannuation balances exceeding $3 million
claims.short_explanation: The 15% Division 296 tax applies only to the earnings attributable to superannuation balances above the $3m threshold, not the entire balance.
claims.detailed_explanation: Division 296 (the 'Better Targeted Super Concessions' measure) does not impose a 15% tax on the entire superannuation balance for accounts exceeding $3 million. Instead, it applies a 15% tax on the earnings proportion that relates to the portion of an individual's Total Superannuation Balance (TSB) exceeding the Low Balance Super Threshold (LSBT) of $3 million. For example, a $4 million balance does not incur $600,000 in tax (15% × $4m); rather, only the earnings attributable to the $1 million excess would be subject to the 15% tax. This distinction is significant because it means the actual tax liability for most affected members is considerably lower than commonly reported, and the tax is based on earnings, not the principal balance.

claims.claim: negative gearing has been fully abolished for all investors
claims.short_explanation: Negative gearing has not been fully abolished. It remains available for existing property investors and is restricted to new builds only from 1 July 2027.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim that negative gearing has been fully abolished is inaccurate. Under the 2026 Budget measures, negative gearing is being restricted to newly constructed residential properties only, effective 1 July 2027. Properties purchased before 7:30pm on Budget Night (12 May 2026) are grandfathered, meaning existing negative gearing arrangements remain intact for those investors. This represents a significant reform rather than an abolition of negative gearing, and existing property investors are largely unaffected by the change.

claims.claim: Inflation indexation always produces a better CGT outcome than the 50% discount for long-held assets
claims.short_explanation: For high-growth assets, the 50% discount can produce a lower effective tax rate than inflation indexation, depending on the investor's marginal tax rate and asset performance.
claims.detailed_explanation: Analysis by the ASX shows that for a retired investor on a 16% marginal tax rate, the 50% CGT discount results in an effective 8% tax on nominal gains, compared to 30% on indexed gains under inflation indexation rules. While inflation indexation adjusts gains for purchasing power erosion, the 50% discount applies to the full nominal gain. For assets with significant nominal growth, the percentage reduction from the 50% discount often exceeds the inflation adjustment benefit. The optimal approach depends on the asset's performance, the investor's marginal rate, and holding period. Neither method universally outperforms the other across all scenarios.

claims.claim: Division 296 imposes a 15% tax on all superannuation balances exceeding $3 million
claims.short_explanation: Division 296 taxes only the earnings attributable to superannuation balances over $3 million, not the entire balance.
claims.detailed_explanation: Division 296 does not impose a 15% levy on total superannuation balances exceeding $3 million. Instead, it applies a 15% tax on the taxable superannuation earnings (TSB) that relate to the portion of a person's balance exceeding the Low Balance Super Threshold (LSBT) of $3 million. The ATO explicitly states the tax is applied 'on the proportion of earnings relating to your TSB that exceeds the LSBT'. This means only the investment returns attributable to the amount above $3 million are subject to the additional 15% tax. For example, a person with a $4 million balance would only pay the extra tax on the earnings related to the $1 million above the threshold, not on the entire $4 million. Media coverage frequently oversimplifies this as a direct tax on balances, which significantly overstates the actual financial impact on affected individuals.

claims.claim: Capital gains will face a new minimum 30% tax rate on ALL gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum tax functions as a floor on the effective tax rate after inflation indexation, not a flat 30% tax on nominal gains. Investors with low inflation or short holding periods may face different outcomes.
claims.detailed_explanation: The 2026-27 Budget introduces changes to capital gains tax (CGT) treatment. The 50% CGT discount is replaced with an inflation-based discount, and a minimum 30% tax rate applies to indexed gains. The mechanism works by calculating the indexed gain (adjusting for inflation) and then applying a 30% floor to the effective tax rate. This is fundamentally different from a flat 30% tax on nominal gains for all investors. An investor with low inflation or a short holding period may have a lower effective tax rate than 30%, while one with high inflation over a long period would face the 30% floor. Media coverage often omits the 'indexed' qualifier, which may mislead investors about their actual tax liability under the new rules.

claims.claim: Inflation indexation always produces a better CGT outcome than the 50% discount for long-held assets
claims.short_explanation: The benefit of inflation indexation over the 50% CGT discount depends on the cumulative inflation rate and holding period. For assets held during low-inflation periods or for moderate time periods, the 50% discount may be equally or more beneficial.
claims.detailed_explanation: While inflation indexation adjusts the cost base of an asset for cumulative inflation since acquisition, effectively inflating away a portion of the nominal capital gain, the 50% CGT discount simply halves the taxable gain regardless of inflation. The relative benefit of each mechanism varies significantly based on context. For assets held through periods of high cumulative inflation (particularly pre-1999 assets where indexation is still available), indexation can produce superior outcomes. However, for assets acquired after 1999 where only the 50% discount applies, or for assets held during extended periods of low inflation, the discount mechanism may deliver equal or better effective tax treatment. The ATO's guidance confirms these are distinct mechanisms with different interaction effects depending on the inflation environment and holding period length.

claims.claim: Division 296 imposes a 15% tax on all superannuation balances exceeding $3 million
claims.short_explanation: Division 296 taxes the proportion of taxable superannuation earnings attributable to balances above the $3m threshold, not a flat 15% on the entire balance over $3m.
claims.detailed_explanation: According to official ATO sources, Division 296 applies a 15% tax on the proportion of taxable superannuation earnings that relates to the total superannuation balance (TSB) exceeding $3 million—not a flat 15% on the entire balance over $3m. This is a significant legal and mathematical distinction. For example, a person with a $4m balance does not pay 15% on $4m (which would be $600k), but rather 15% on the notional earnings attributable to the $1m excess portion. The $3m threshold operates as a proxy for determining how much of an individual's superannuation earnings should be subject to the additional 15% tax. This technical oversimplification in media reporting overstates the actual tax burden by orders of magnitude and misrepresents the legislative mechanism.

claims.claim: 30% minimum tax on ALL capital gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The minimum 30% applies to real capital gains above inflation after cost-base indexation, not to nominal capital gains.
claims.detailed_explanation: The 2026-27 Budget introduces reforms replacing the CGT discount with inflation-based cost-base indexation. Under these reforms, capital gains are first adjusted for inflation before calculating tax liability. The minimum 30% tax rate applies to the real gains (gains above inflation), not to the full nominal value of the asset. A taxpayer with genuine economic losses or gains merely matching inflation would not face the 30% minimum on nominal values. Media reports stating 'tax on ALL capital gains' or '30% on all gains' oversimplify the policy — the minimum rate only applies to inflation-adjusted gains.

claims.claim: More than half of the benefit of the CGT concession went to the top 1% of income earners
claims.short_explanation: The specific statistic cannot be verified as the source data year, methodology for identifying the 'top 1%', and data source (Treasury or ATO) are not specified in the original reporting.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim appears in The Guardian but lacks critical contextual information needed for verification. No financial year is cited for the underlying data, making it impossible to cross-reference against official Treasury tax expenditure reports or ATO taxation statistics. Additionally, the methodology for defining the 'top 1%' (whether by income, wealth, or CGT gains received) is not specified. Different definitional approaches can yield significantly different results. Without access to the underlying dataset and methodology notes, this specific percentage claim cannot be independently verified or disputed.

claims.claim: housing measures cost $6.4bn over four years
claims.short_explanation: The $6.4 billion figure appears in multiple media sources but lacks official confirmation on budget.gov.au as a standalone 'cost'. It may represent the gross spending package rather than net cost.
claims.detailed_explanation: While the $6.4 billion figure is cited across numerous media outlets, the KPMG implementation review mentions $47.5 million specifically for Treasury and ATO implementation costs. The $6.4bn figure likely refers to the total gross spending on housing measures including infrastructure, while administrative implementation costs ($47.5m) are listed separately. Additionally, CGT changes may generate offsetting revenue that reduces the net cost. Sources may be conflating different budget line items, gross costs versus net costs after projected revenue, or the total package versus individual components. Without official budget.gov.au confirmation categorising this as the definitive cost figure, the claim remains unverified.

claims.claim: Budget allocates $47.5 million for CGT implementation
claims.short_explanation: The $47.5 million figure appears in official budget documents, but reporting varies on whether it covers CGT only or broader reform scope, and whether it represents total or annual funding.
claims.detailed_explanation: The $47.5 million figure for CGT reform implementation does appear in official budget documentation. However, significant discrepancies exist in how this figure is reported. Some sources cite the amount specifically for 'CGT implementation' while others reference it in the context of 'CGT and negative gearing reform implementation.' KPMG Budget Analysis indicates that a detailed breakdown exists showing ATO and Treasury resource allocation, which may differ from simplified media reporting. Additionally, the timeframe requires clarification - it is unclear whether this represents the total allocation across all years or an annual figure repeated over the four-year budget period. The discrepancy between CGT-only and broader reform scope reporting suggests the original figure may encompass more than just capital gains tax changes.
